Among replicate genotypes of Drosophila melanogaster, inter-genotypic variation in the slope of individual thermal-death-time curves generates a fanning-out effect that causes the variance in log(failure time) to increase with temperature independently of changes in mean thermal tolerance.

In ectotherms, the observed increase in variance of log failure times at higher stressful temperatures is generated by among-individual or genotype-specific variation in the slope of the log failure time–temperature relationship, so that clones or isogenic lines derived from the same population will show genotype-by-temperature interactions in failure-time variance across stressful temperatures.

In *Drosophila melanogaster*, isogenic lines with greater genetic variation in the slope of the individual thermal-death-time curve will show steeper increases in variance of log failure times across stressful temperatures, because genotype-specific temperature sensitivities cause failure times to fan out at higher temperatures.

Within-population genetic variation in the slope of individual thermal-death-time curves generates a “fanning-out” effect that drives the observed increase in variance of log failure times with temperature, and genotype-specific TDT models will more accurately predict survival under fluctuating heat stress than population-average models.

Individuals within a population vary genetically in the slope of their thermal death time curves, and this among-genotype variation increases the variance of log failure times more at high than at intermediate stressful temperatures.

Isogenic Drosophila lines will show greater among-genotype variance in thermal-death-time slopes at extreme high temperatures, indicating that cryptic genetic variation contributes to the population-level increase in variance of log failure times.
